title: The Ravidassia community
hookLine: a community who revere Guru Ravidas and now keep their own scripture

cards: A hymn in the Guru Granth Sahib carries the name Ravidas, the poet tradition remembers as a shoemaker of Benares. In a gurdwara, it's sung as one voice among many in a great book.

Across town, under a different symbol, the same words are sung as the voice of the one the room calls Guru. Same poet, same words, a different center. Year three met the community who keep Ravidas at that center.
Since then, something has changed in how they keep him.

teach.b: First, who they are. The Ravidassia community revere Guru Ravidas as their Guru. It includes families from the same communities Ravidas came from, the ones the old order counted low.
For them, a shoemaker who sang his way past every wall of caste is not one voice among many. He is the voice. Second, what has changed.
For a long time, the Guru Granth Sahib was installed in Ravidassia places of worship, just as in a gurdwara.

In recent years, the community has gathered Guru Ravidas's own hymns into a scripture of their own, and now install it at the center of their worship, with their own greeting and their own symbol too.
Third, a hymn to hold it all. In the Granth, in Raag Sorath, Ravidas sings a chain of pictures to God, in paraphrase: you are the sandalwood, I am the water. You are the cloud, I am the peacock.
You are the lamp, I am the wick. You are the master, I am the servant. In each pair, the lesser thing is never thrown away.
Water takes the scent of sandalwood. The wick is what lets the lamp burn. A low thing, held close to God, becomes part of the light.
Fourth, how to stand toward this. Sikhs keep singing Ravidas in the Granth with full honor. The Ravidassia community keep him at the center of a path that is now their own.
Some on both sides feel the parting deeply; others call it a community finding its own name.
Neither story needs ranking. The same hymns are still sung in both houses.

how: The Ravidassia community revere Guru Ravidas as their Guru and keep a scripture of his hymns in their places of worship; Sikhs continue to sing Ravidas's hymns as part of the Guru Granth Sahib.

practice: Bring to mind a group that once shared a home with yours, a congregation, a club, a circle of friends, and then went its own way, and let anything that still stings be there.
Then picture them at their own table, singing their own song, and wish them well there. If you pray, you can rest on Waheguru.
